questions.text: What exactly is the 'managed secret store' (which product), and what is 'workload identity'? How does a pod prove it is orders-api-prod to the store?
Who or what actually triggers the rolling deploy and builds the image? Is 'operator starts the deploy' a manual command, and what tool does it use?
questions.about: Step 7. Rolling deploy of v2 to prod

questions.text: In Step 7, Moves says each new pod loads keys then binds the port, but B2 says the port is bound only after the cache is stored. How does readiness (/healthz) relate to this, and what does the rollout wait on?
questions.about: Step 7 and B5. Readiness and liveness

questions.text: Step 4 removes api_key from config/app.yaml, but how do old v1 pods get key A? Are they still running images with A baked in, and do they ever read the store?
questions.about: Step 7. Old v1 pods keep serving with key A

questions.text: What does the on-call do when writing B to the store: which tool or console, and how does a store write produce a version id that the refresher compares?
questions.about: Step 5. Rotate at providers and write new prod values

questions.text: If a refresh finds a changed version id, and a provider call is in flight, what does the client use? Also, after refresh failures continue for hours, what happens to the pod and to calls when the key is later revoked?
Step 8 says confirm each pod logged B version ids at startup. Where do these logs come from and how does startup log them, since B2 does not mention logging versions?
What is 'temporary compatibility code' in Step 11? Nothing in Parts A or B describes any such code being added.
Step 3 says dev uses the engineer's identity via make run. How does a laptop get that identity, and how does the loader know it is in dev mode versus prod?

answers.text: The brief names only 'our managed secret store' and does not name the product, nor the mechanism a pod uses to prove its identity. Workload identity is described in the file only as the identity the cluster gives the pod, which the store checks. Logged as open question 1. Changed: Terms section now defines both terms in plain words, and the file states that no static credentials are stored on disk.

deploy.md says rollouts are rolling with maxUnavailable 0 and that CI builds the image, but it does not name the deploy tool or who starts a rollout. The plan says an operator starts it after Step 6 is approved. The tool is logged as open question 2.

Readiness is GET /healthz returning 200. The port is not bound until the three keys are loaded (B2 step 6), so a new pod with no keys is not reachable and is never ready. The rollout waits on readiness, so a pod that cannot load keys halts it. Changed: Step 7 now says the pod reads keys, binds the port, and /healthz returns 200 only after that; B5 says the same thing and explains why.

v1 pods run the old image, which has key A in config/app.yaml baked in (deploy.md: the image includes config/app.yaml as it is in the repo). They never read the store. Step 4 changes only the branch and the v2 image. The earlier draft said v1 pods pick up B within 5 minutes, which was wrong. Changed: Step 5 now says only v2 pods refresh and v1 pods keep A. The Step 9 gate 'no pod runs the v1 digest' is what makes revoking A safe.

The tool or console the on-call uses to write B is not known. The mechanism the plan relies on is that the store returns a version id on each write, and the refresher compares the id it last loaded with the id the store returns. Logged as open question 3. Changed: Step 5 names the ticket record and the provider-console check; B4 states the comparison.

A provider call keeps the value it read when the call started, so a swap during the call does not change it (stated in B3). If refresh fails for hours, the pod keeps its last good value and keeps serving; readiness stays green (B5). If that value is later revoked, calls fail with 401 or 403 until a refresh gets a newer version. This trade-off is stated in the failure table. The staleness alert (open question 7) and the 401 immediate-refresh option (open question 6) are the mitigations, and the owner decides them.

B2 did not say the pod logs version ids. Changed: B2 step 4 now logs the version id of each loaded secret at startup, so Step 8 can check for them. The logs are the pod's own startup logs, sent to the central log service (deploy.md).

No compatibility code is planned. Nothing in Part A or Part B adds temporary code, and no fallback reads keys from the yaml. The Step 11 entry was a leftover and is removed. The tracking issue is closed in Step 10.

How a laptop gets the engineer's identity is not known, because the brief does not name the store's authentication method. The decided part is the mode selection: make run sets APP_ENV=dev, the loader reads prod only when APP_ENV=prod, and only pods set that (B9). Logged as open question 3.

teachbacks.text:
1. Starting point (today). `config/app.yaml` is committed to git and copied into every image. It holds three live provider keys (payments, email, geocoding). The app reads the file once at start and copies each key into its client. Changing a key needs a new image and a redeploy. The document calls the current key "key A" and treats it as leaked. The migration moves the keys into a managed secret store under `orders-api/<env>/<name>`.

2. Step 1, inventory (kickoff). Someone lists every user of key A: prod pods, CI jobs, local runs, scripts, other services and provider-side integrations. They confirm that each provider accepts two active keys at once (the blocking "overlap gate"). They also list every v1 image in the registry. The only state is a tracking issue with no key values. If a provider fails the gate, work stops for that provider. A consumer that can't be found blocks only Step 9.

3. Step 2, store paths and access policy. `orders-api/dev/*` and `orders-api/prod/*` are created. The store's access policy says: the `orders-api-prod` identity reads only prod paths; only the security on-call role writes prod; engineers read dev only and can't read or list prod. Automated allow/deny tests for each identity must pass before Step 5. If engineers can read prod, or the prod identity can read another path, stop.

4. Step 3, dev setup. Sandbox keys are created at each provider that offers them and written to `orders-api/dev/*`. `make run` sets `APP_ENV=dev` and loads dev values through the same loader with the engineer's identity. An offline mode with stub provider clients is added. Anyone without dev access, or using a provider with no sandbox, uses offline mode. Nobody falls back to prod.

5. Step 4, code change on a branch (nothing deployed). Part B is implemented on a branch, and `api_key` is removed from the yaml. The CI guard goes on the same branch. Tests run in dev. They cover startup retries and exit, refresh replacing a value, a failed refresh keeping the old value and logging a warning, clients reading the current value, and no secrets in logs, repr or exceptions. Failing tests block the merge, and customers are unaffected.

6. Step 5, create key B and put it in prod. This starts when Step 4 is green and the security on-call is available. For each provider the on-call creates key B while A stays active. They write B to `orders-api/prod/<name>` and record the version ids (never the values) in the change ticket. They check in the provider console that B is active. If B creation or the store write fails, A still works and they retry. A bad B is replaced by writing a new version. The running v1 pods hold A in memory from their image and don't read the store, so this step doesn't affect them.

7. Step 6, merge and build v2. This happens only after Step 5 is recorded. The PR merges to `main`, and CI builds the v2 image. The v2 config has no `api_key`, and the CI guard is on. The guard parses the yaml and fails on any `api_key`, scans changed files for the `pk_live_`, `ml_live_` and `geo_live_` prefixes and for a literal `api_key:`, and scans the built image's config. The image is stored in the registry and identified by its digest. If CI fails after the merge, don't deploy v2; fix forward.

8. Step 7, rollout, and what one v2 pod does at startup.
   - An operator starts the deploy. A rolling update replaces one pod at a time with `maxUnavailable: 0`.
   - The new pod reads the non-secret yaml (app name, port, log level, base URLs, timeouts, from address). `APP_ENV` comes from a deployment setting (B1).
   - It creates a store client using its workload identity, `orders-api-prod`. No credentials are stored on disk.
   - It fetches the three secrets. On failure it retries 3 times, 2 seconds apart, then logs the error without values and exits non-zero.
   - It puts each value in the in-memory SecretCache with its version id and fetch time, atomically, and logs each version id.
   - It starts the refresher.
   - Only then does it bind the HTTP port. `/healthz` returns 200 only after that, so a listening pod always has keys.
   - If the store is unreachable or access is denied, the pod exits and never becomes ready. The rollout halts and old v1 pods keep serving with key A. Fix the identity or network problem and redeploy; don't force it.
   - During the rollout, A pods and B pods run together, which is why the overlap gate exists.
   - If a provider returns 401 or 403 to v2 pods, halt and roll back to v1. Key A is still active, so v1 works.

9. Runtime request handling. `PaymentsClient`, `EmailClient` and `GeocodingClient` hold a reference to the cache rather than a copy of the key. Each outgoing provider call reads the current value from the cache. A call that has already read a value keeps it even if a refresh swaps in a new one mid-call. If a provider returns 401 or 403, the app logs the status and the version id in use, never the key. A redaction filter keeps `Authorization` headers and key-bearing request bodies out of logs, tracebacks and HTTP debug output.

10. Refresh loop (B4). A timer fires every 300 seconds, with small random jitter. It fetches all three secrets. If a version id has changed, it swaps in the new value and logs `rotated <name> to version <id>`. If the fetch fails, it keeps the last good value, logs a warning (secret name, version id in use, error class, no values), and tries again next cycle. A metric exposes the time since the last successful refresh. A store outage after startup does not change readiness, and the pod keeps serving. Liveness is separate and doesn't depend on the store.

11. Step 8, verify and soak. This starts when all 4 pods run v2. Confirm every pod runs the v2 digest and logged its version ids at startup. Confirm the provider 401/403 rate stays at baseline. Then hold a soak period longer than one 5-minute refresh cycle plus the rollback window. Evidence comes from central logs (30-day retention), deploy status and provider dashboards. If any pod still runs v1 or lacks version ids, don't start Step 9.

12. Step 9, revoke key A. This starts after the soak passes and every Step 1 consumer is confirmed off A. The security on-call revokes A at one provider at a time, after that provider's checks pass: no pod on the v1 digest, no consumer using A, and dev and CI using no live keys. Revocation usually can't be undone. If a missed consumer breaks, issue a new key D and write it to the prod path. v2 pods pick it up within 5 minutes without a restart. After this, v1 is no longer a rollback target. A pod holding a revoked key gets 401/403 until a refresh brings a newer version, and readiness stays green meanwhile.

13. Step 10, clean up. Remove copies of A from working copies, CI variables and `.env` files. Scan the repo, built images and central logs for the three key prefixes. Mark v1 images do-not-deploy but keep them for audit. Don't rewrite git history. Close the tracking issue. Leftover copies are already revoked, so there is no customer impact; record them and escalate to security.

14. Safety nets in code. At startup the loader exits non-zero if the yaml contains an `api_key` at any depth (B8). Values live only in the SecretCache. They are never put in environment variables, temp files, an on-disk cache or subprocesses. Core dumps are disabled where the platform allows (B7).
gaps: The document does not name the secret store product or how a pod proves its workload identity to it, so I can't say how the store client authenticates in step 8.
The deploy tool and who triggers the Step 7 rollout are not specified.
The tool the security on-call uses to write keys to the store is not specified. How engineers authenticate for dev reads is also not specified.

How the app learns a version id has changed in the refresh is only described as comparing version ids. The document does not say whether the refresher fetches and compares all three at once or each separately, or what happens if only some of the three fetches succeed.
Whether the exact retry count at startup is one attempt plus 3 retries or 3 attempts total is not settled (Open question 4).
The exact secret names for email and geocoding are assumed, not confirmed.
Whether a 401 from a provider triggers an immediate refresh and a retry is undecided, so I can't say what a v2 pod does on a 401 beyond logging it.
The soak length, the rollback window and the staleness alert threshold are not set, so I can't say when Step 8 ends or when someone is alerted to a stale cache.
The document doesn't say how a rollback to v1 is carried out (which tool or command), or how 'rolling back' works when the deploy method is undefined.

It does not say how the Step 5 prod key write reaches pods already running v2, or what happens to old v1 pods after Step 9 revokes A if any remain, beyond saying they would fail until replaced. It also does not say whether the 5-minute refresh could pick up a half-written or bad B before checks run.
Key rotation cadence after migration is undecided by security, so no scheduled rotation flow exists to explain.
